newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Colston corruption row hits Australia govt - polls.
newsitem.headline: Colston corruption row hits Australia govt - polls.

text.p: The scandal over corruption allegations against a key independent Australian senator has undermined public support for the ruling Coalition government, according o two polls published on Tuesday.
In a poll in the Bulletin newsweekly, 72 percent of voters said the affair had damaged the government.

A separate poll in The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper found that 23 percent of voters would be less inclined to vote for the Coalition and 36 percent said the affair had worsened their attitude to the Liberal-National government.
Police are investigating Colston, whose support is crucial to government reforms passing the upper house Senate, over allegations of travel allowance abuse.
The government, Labor opposition and Australian Democrats, the third power bloc in the Senate, have demanded he step aside from the powerful post of Senate deputy president.
All have said they would dump Colston from the position if he has not moved by the time the Senate resumes on May 6.
Labor and the Democrats are also seeking his resignation from parliament altogether, a move that would cast doubt over future government reforms.
Colston, who denies any illegal activity, is in a Brisbane hospital suffering from a lung infection and has rejected all calls to act, saying he will make a decision after he recovers.
Prime Minister John Howard's year-old government does not have a majority in the Senate and relies on Colston and another independent to pass critical measures, including budget cuts.
Colston, elected as a Labor senator, defected from the party last year to sit as an independent and would have to be replaced by a Labor member if he was forced out of the Senate.
This would make it more difficult for the government to win the two extra votes in needs to pass legislation, although Labor would also still be short of a Senate majority.
